extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of Renaissance literature and political/moral philosophy (e.g., scholars of Castiglione)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the normative qualities and prescriptive standards for princes and courtiers as discussed in Book IV of The Courtier (Castiglione) — i.e., what makes a 'good prince' and a 'perfect courtier' according to the dialogue. The excerpt offers behavioral, moral, and practical desiderata rather than a formal scoring rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Princely attention to small matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The prince should 'take care to heed not only the matters already mentioned, but those which are much smaller, and as far as possible understand all details affecting his people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not leave all affairs to a single minister; the prince must be informed about even minor details because 'there is no man who is very apt for all things' and excessive credulity in rulers causes great harm. Exercise judgment to perceive who deserves belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentrating power in a single minister
rubrics_metrics.description: The prince should 'not ever so believe or trust any one of his ministers as to confide to that one alone the bridle and control of all his government.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegation is necessary but dangerous if total; spread oversight to avoid harm caused by credulity toward a single advisor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active oversight of ministers and dispute resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The prince should 'understand the acts and be the overseer of his ministers; to settle and shorten disputes among his subjects; to be the means of making peace among them, and of allying them in marriage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical governance duties: hands-on supervision, arbitration of conflicts, and fostering social/political alliances for stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster civic prosperity and social order
rubrics_metrics.description: The prince should have 'his city all united and agreed in friendship like a private family, populous, not poor, peaceful, full of good artificers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should aim for population, economic health, peace, skilled craftsmen — i.e., an internally cohesive and prosperous polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support commerce and hospitality
rubrics_metrics.description: The prince should 'favour merchants and even to aid them with money; to be generous and splendid in hospitality towards foreigners and ecclesiastics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic encouragement of trade and conspicuous hospitality are recommended as princely duties that strengthen the realm and its reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of superfluities to prevent ruin
rubrics_metrics.description: The prince should 'moderate all superfluities' — set limits 'upon the too sumptuous houses of private folk, upon feasts, upon the excessive doweries of women, upon their luxury, upon their display in jewels and vesture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small-seeming extravagances can lead to civic decline; regulate private excesses that harm public welfare and moral order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtier's primary aim: to instruct the prince toward virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier's aim is 'to make the prince virtuous' — to allure him to 'many virtues, like justice, generosity, magnanimity' and to lead him toward virtuous habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The courtier need not be sole cause of virtue (success depends on the prince's nature), but must be capable of instructing and preventing corruption (e.g., opposing flatterers and slanderers). Virtue is achieved in action, and the courtier works by influencing deeds and habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtier should know the prince's character and enter tactfully
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier's office is 'to know the prince's character and inclinations, and thus to enter tactfully into his favour according to need and opportunity... and then to lead him towards virtue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective instruction requires psychological insight and tactful access; use safe means and timing to influence the prince (Aristotle/Plato cited as exemplars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtier's breadth of accomplishments and qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier is ascribed many accomplishments and virtues: 'jousting and other exercises of the person... music and dancing and festivals and games and love-making' as well as 'gentleness of behaviour, discretion, capacity, eagerness for honour, magnanimity, courtesy, generosity, love of justice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A perfect courtier blends physical, artistic, social, and moral accomplishments — but these need not conflict with wisdom or discretion; they must serve the aim of influencing the prince.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-appropriate practice vs. understanding of accomplishments
rubrics_metrics.description: If an older Courtier cannot practice youthful exercises (arms, dancing, music), 'it does not prevent his understanding them' and 'if he has practised them in his youth, it does not prevent his having the more perfect judgment regarding them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical experience earlier in life plus mature judgment can substitute for current physical display; teaching and understanding are acceptable ways to fulfill courtier functions at older ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtier should avoid service to inveterately wicked princes
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Courtier finds himself 'in the service of a prince of so evil a disposition... he ought to escape that bondage, in order not to receive blame for his lord's evil deeds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral integrity may require withdrawal rather than complicity; attempting Courtiership on hopelessly corrupt rulers is both futile and blameworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of a courtier's influence (dependence on prince's nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: The courtier's success depends on whether the prince is by nature inclined and fitted to be virtuous; if not, 'all the Courtier's care and reminders would be in vain' (analogy of husbandman and barren sand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of a courtier should account for structural limits: inability to change an intrinsically unteachable prince is not a failure of method but of subject suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as habit produced by action
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Our habits are what our actions make them, and virtue consists in action' — so the courtier aims to induce virtuous actions in the prince that become habitual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes practical/behavioral change rather than mere instruction; the courtier's role includes prompting acts that can be adopted and repeated by the prince.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of love for the Courtier (rational vs. sensual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Love is defined as 'a certain desire to enjoy beauty.' If guided by sense it leads to 'false and vicious' possession and unhappiness; if guided by reason (choice/intellect) it is 'most good and holy' and more fitting for maturer persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For courtiers (especially older ones), love should be governed by reason — desire for beauty as understood and chosen, not mere sensual appetite. Sensual love causes satiety, hatred, or endless longing; rational love yields true possession and good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Youths' sensual love: excused but to be moderated
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensual love in the young is common and often excusable because of human frailty; though it brings anguish and danger, it can motivate some worthy acts, and youths who 'control their appetites and love in reason' are commended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forgiveness for youthful excess is conditional on courtesy, gentleness, and worth, and requires abandoning sensuality in later life; persistent sensuality into maturity deserves strong blame.
